config.title: Discriminated Union Props

intro.title: Discriminated Union Props
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that displays different types of notifications, such as success, warning, and error messages. You'll learn how to use discriminated union props, a pattern in TypeScript and JavaScript that helps ensure type safety by using a common property (like 'type') to distinguish between different possible shapes of props. The main technologies involved are React functional components, JSX for rendering, and conditional rendering based on the prop's discriminant. This approach makes your components more predictable and easier to maintain by clearly defining the data they can receive.
intro.usecase: Discriminated union props are essential for building robust, type-safe UI components that can render in multiple distinct states. For example, a dashboard card might display as a loading skeleton, an error message, or a data visualization—each requiring different props and structure. This pattern is commonly used in form steps, modals with different content types, or navigation menus with icon-only and text-and-icon variants, ensuring the component only receives valid props for its current mode.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript discriminated union type to define component props with distinct variants
Implement a React component that accepts and destructures discriminated union props
Configure conditional rendering logic based on the discriminant property of union props
Initialize and manipulate component state that works with discriminated union prop variants
Apply type narrowing techniques to safely access variant-specific properties within handlers
Integrate event handlers that update UI based on the active discriminated union variant
Render multiple component instances with different discriminated union prop configurations

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define the component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure it returns a JSX div element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns a JSX div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your component is named App and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns a div.

steps.title: Initialize state for the selected type
steps.instruction: Inside your component, use useState to initialize a state variable named 'selectedType' with a default value of 'info'.
steps.hint: Call useState with the string 'info' and destructure the returned array into two variables: the state variable and its setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state with a string
const [message, setMessage] = useState('hello');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'selectedType' initialized to 'info'.
successCriteria: The component contains a useState call that declares 'selectedType' with initial value 'info'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with the exact variable name 'selectedType' and initial value 'info'.
steps.feedbackWrong: declare a state variable inside the component using useState.

steps.title: Define the union data structure
steps.instruction: Inside your component (above the return statement), define an object named 'messageData' that contains three different message types: 'info', 'warning', and 'error', each with distinct properties.
steps.hint: Create a plain JavaScript object with keys for each message type. Each type should have different property names to make them distinct.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a messageData object with three distinct message structures that can be used later based on the selected type.
successCriteria: The messageData object is defined with 'info', 'warning', and 'error' keys, each having different properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have all three message types (info, warning, error) with different properties for each.
steps.feedbackWrong: The messageData object should contain three different message types with distinct properties. Try creating an object with keys 'info', 'warning', and 'error', each with different property names.

steps.title: Create a handler to change the selected type
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named 'handleTypeChange' that takes a 'type' parameter and updates the 'selectedType' state with that value.
steps.hint: Define a function that calls setSelectedType with the provided type argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handler function that updates the selectedType state when called with a new type.
successCriteria: The component contains a function named handleTypeChange that accepts a type parameter and calls setSelectedType with that parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named handleTypeChange, accepts a type parameter, and calls setSelectedType with that parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function named handleTypeChange that takes a type parameter and updates the selectedType state using setSelectedType.

steps.title: Create the MessageDisplay component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named MessageDisplay that accepts props with type and message properties. The component should return a div element.
steps.hint: Define the component with a function declaration or arrow function that takes a single parameter (props). Destructure type and message from props, or access them directly via props.type and props.message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component is defined and ready to receive props with type and message properties.
successCriteria: A component named MessageDisplay is created, accepts props, and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the MessageDisplay component. Make sure it accepts props and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The MessageDisplay component is not properly defined. Create a functional component named MessageDisplay that accepts props and returns a div.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering logic in MessageDisplay
steps.instruction: Inside the MessageDisplay component, add conditional rendering logic that returns different JSX based on the type prop value ('info', 'warning', or 'error').
steps.hint: Use if/else or switch statements to check the type prop and return appropriate JSX for each case.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component now has conditional logic that will render different content based on the type prop.
successCriteria: MessageDisplay component contains conditional logic (if/else or switch) that returns different JSX for 'info', 'warning', and 'error' type values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your conditional logic covers all three type values ('info', 'warning', 'error') and returns appropriate JSX for each case.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering logic is missing or incomplete. Add logic that checks the type prop and returns different JSX for 'info', 'warning', and 'error' values.

steps.title: Add the control buttons in App
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add three buttons with labels 'Info', 'Warning', and 'Error'. Each button should have an onClick handler that calls handleTypeChange with the corresponding type string ('info', 'warning', 'error').
steps.hint: Create button elements with onClick handlers that call handleTypeChange with the appropriate type value. Remember to wrap multiple elements in a fragment or container.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: buttons with click handlers
<>
  <button onClick={() => setMode('light')}>Light</button>
  <button onClick={() => setMode('dark')}>Dark</button>
</>
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will render three interactive buttons that allow the user to change the selected message type.
successCriteria: Three buttons are present with labels 'Info', 'Warning', and 'Error', each with onClick handlers calling handleTypeChange with the correct type string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have all three buttons with correct labels and onClick handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons aren't set up correctly. Check that you have three buttons with proper labels and onClick handlers calling handleTypeChange.

steps.title: Render the MessageDisplay component
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, render the MessageDisplay component and pass the selectedType state as the 'type' prop.
steps.hint: Add <MessageDisplay type={selectedType} /> inside the fragment where you want the message to appear.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component will be rendered in the App component with the current selectedType passed as a prop.
successCriteria: MessageDisplay component is rendered in App's return statement with type={selectedType} prop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're passing the selectedType state as the 'type' prop to MessageDisplay.
steps.feedbackWrong: The MessageDisplay component needs to be rendered with the selectedType passed as a prop. Try adding <MessageDisplay type={selectedType} /> inside the fragment.

steps.title: Add styling to distinguish message types
steps.instruction: In the MessageDisplay component, add inline styles to give each message type a distinct visual appearance. Use the 'type' prop to conditionally apply different styles for 'info', 'warning', and 'error' messages.
steps.hint: You can add a style object inside the component and apply it to the message container. Use conditional logic (like a switch statement or if-else) to set different style properties based on the 'type' prop value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component will apply different visual styles (like background color, text color, or border) to messages based on their type, making it easy to distinguish between info, warning, and error messages.
successCriteria: MessageDisplay uses inline styles that change based on the 'type' prop, with distinct appearances for 'info', 'warning', and 'error' types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but it doesn't fully distinguish all three message types. Make sure you have different styles for 'info', 'warning', and 'error' messages based on the 'type' prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The MessageDisplay component doesn't have conditional styling based on the 'type' prop. Add inline styles that change depending on whether the type is 'info', 'warning', or 'error'.
